text: Johnson's Preface begins its praise of Shakespeare with a principle, and the rest of the argument depends on it: "Nothing can please many, and please long, but just representations of general nature" (Johnson 1765). A writer who copies the manners of his own town and season may be admired while those manners last. When they pass, his figures pass with them, and a later reader finds little left but the costume. Johnson places Shakespeare above the dramatists of his age on exactly this ground. His persons are drawn from what men share in every country and every generation; they act from passions that move all minds, and the accidents of local custom lie lightly upon them. A reader who has never walked an Elizabethan street can therefore recognise the jealousy of a husband or the vanity of an old father, and can judge whether the speech is fitted to the feeling. Johnson's test is endurance, and the plays had already met it by the time he wrote; the comedies of fashion that had crowded the same stages were by then read, if at all, for their curiosities, while Shakespeare's people were still taken for the truth.
